analysis.one_liner: Requires large tax-exempt hospitals to disclose finances, charity care, lobbying, and drug-discount profits to the IRS.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee voted 25–15 on July 1, 2026 to advance a bill requiring tax-exempt hospitals to report detailed finances to the IRS; no House floor vote has occurred yet.
analysis.plain_summary: Nonprofit hospitals pay no federal income tax, and in exchange they are supposed to provide financial assistance and serve community health needs. This bill would force them to file detailed reports with the IRS: how much charity care they actually gave, how many assistance applications they granted or denied, what they spend on advertising, lobbying, and administration, how much money they make on each service line, and how much they profit from the federal 340B drug discount program. It would also require the Government Accountability Office to estimate how much tax the 25 highest-revenue hospital systems would pay if they lost their tax exemption. The bill does not raise taxes or penalize anyone; it requires disclosure.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers. Charity-care patients would gain visibility into how many applications hospitals grant versus deny; taxpayers would finally see, in one place, whether large nonprofit hospitals are earning their exemptions through community benefit or spending it on advertising, lobbying, and administration. The 340B disclosures would show how much profit hospitals capture from a drug discount program meant to help low-income patients.

how_it_helps.text: Every tax-exempt hospital must report with its IRS return how it is addressing the needs in its community health assessment, which needs it is not addressing and why, its audited financial statements, the value of financial assistance provided, and the number of financial assistance applications received, granted, and denied.

Large hospitals (more than 100 staffed inpatient beds) must separately report, facility by facility, their spending on their top three community health priorities and on quality improvement versus nonclinical programs, a category the bill defines to include administration, billing, public affairs, government affairs, and lobbying.

High-revenue hospitals (over $100 million in net patient revenue) must report advertising costs, the revenues and costs of each health service line, and — if they participate in the 340B drug discount program — the number of patients served and their net profit margin on 340B drugs.

The Government Accountability Office must study the cost of the new reporting and estimate how much tax the 25 highest-grossing tax-exempt hospital organizations would owe if they were not tax-exempt, giving Congress the numbers it would need to revisit the exemption itself.

analysis.who_pays: Large and high-revenue tax-exempt hospital organizations bear the cost of compiling and reporting this information, including facility-level service line accounting and a standardized HHS service-line taxonomy they must map to. Smaller hospitals face only the basic charity-care reporting, and not until three years after enactment.

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden is real: the bill itself directs the GAO to study the additional cost to hospitals of complying, an acknowledgment that compiling facility-level service line and 340B data will not be free.

Transparency alone changes nothing by itself. The bill explicitly states it creates no inference about whether hospitals deserve their tax exemption and imposes no tax or penalty; its benefits to patients depend entirely on Congress, regulators, or the public acting on what is disclosed.

Honest supporters would acknowledge that money spent on compliance accounting is money not spent on patient care, and that detailed service-line cost allocation across shared staff and facilities is partly a judgment call that hospitals will contest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are administrative and fall on large institutions; the benefit is that the public would finally see, in standardized form, what nonprofit hospitals give back for their tax exemption — including their margins on 340B drugs and their spending on advertising and lobbying. The bill's main weakness is that it stops at disclosure: no penalties, no tax change, and an explicit no-inference clause. Its value depends on what Congress or the public does with the numbers.

outcome.mechanism: The Ways and Means Committee approved the bill at a markup on July 1, 2026 by a 25–15 vote, but the full House has not voted on it and neither has the Senate.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregory Murphy (R-NC) introduced the bill on June 29, 2026 with Rep. Lloyd Smucker as cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The committee held a markup session on July 1, 2026 and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute by a vote of 25–15.
No further action has been taken as of the provided record; the bill still needs a vote by the full House and the Senate, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final winner yet. Because nothing has become law, large tax-exempt hospital systems remain free of the new reporting; the public's gain so far is only that a transparency bill cleared a powerful committee with a clear majority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill awaits a floor vote

for.name: Rep. Gregory F. Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it through the Ways and Means markup.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee majority
for.role: Committee members who voted to report the bill
for.what_they_did: Voted 25–15 at the July 1, 2026 markup to order the bill reported in the nature of a substitute.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee minority (15 no votes)
against.role: Members who voted against ordering the bill reported
against.what_they_did: Voted no at the July 1, 2026 markup, though the bill still advanced 25–15.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows a 25–15 committee vote but no party breakdown; the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are both Republicans.

industries.note: Hospitals with more than 100 staffed beds or over $100 million in net patient revenue would face detailed, facility-level reporting on charity care denials, advertising, lobbying, service line profits, and 340B drug margins, plus compliance costs. Their interest in avoiding this exposure runs against the public's interest in knowing whether they earn their tax exemptions.

industries.industry: Hospitals in the 340B drug discount program
industries.note: High-revenue 340B hospitals must disclose how much they receive from payers above the discounted ceiling price for 340B drugs, exposing margins in a program intended to benefit low-income patients. The bill also requires them to report the costs of participating and creates no inference about the program's proper operation.

industries.industry: Small, rural, and critical access hospitals
industries.note: Critical access hospitals, rural emergency hospitals, and hospitals under the size and revenue thresholds are largely spared the heaviest requirements, and smaller hospitals get a three-year delay on the charity-care reporting. Rural facilities avoid most of the compliance burden.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee but has no floor schedule. Bills that make it out of Ways and Means late in a session sometimes reach the floor, often by suspension of the rules (a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial bills that needs two-thirds support); with an unclear partisan split at markup, its path is uncertain, and if the House does not act before January 3, 2027, it dies and must be reintroduced next Congress.
